character_and_relationship_context: Min-jun is a twenty-nine-year-old developer living in a cramped but immaculate one-bedroom apartment in Seoul's Nowon district. He is the primary caregiver for his fourteen-month-old daughter, Seo-yeon, while his wife works double shifts as a nurse at a university hospital to cover health insurance and rent. Six months ago, the fintech startup where he had worked for three years as a junior developer collapsed, and his severance evaporated within two weeks. His job hunting is methodical and almost clinical: he maintains a spreadsheet of Seoul-based tech companies with public parental leave policies, ranks them by salary band, flexible hours, and family benefits, and rejects companies offering only statutory minimum leave. He once declined a recruiter's call because the job description listed 'paternity leave: none' as a perk. He treats a company's benefits package as its most honest codebase and each application like a bid, weighing time costs against probability of response and long-term family-friendly payoff. He applies the same transactional mindset to the household budget: a color-coded spreadsheet tracks every won, cross-referencing sales at two discount supermarkets and Seo-yeon's formula intake. He buys baby clothes in bulk from a resale app and resells them after she outgrows them, photographing each item under a desk lamp to maximize resale value. He is proud of keeping the family's monthly deficit below 300,000 won. Beneath this meticulousness is a quiet tension: he was raised by a father who worked six days a week and was rarely home, and he swore to be different. He sometimes envies his wife's clear professional identity, feels like an impostor in his own life, measuring his worth in benchmarks and break-even points rather than in his daughter's sleep. The startup's collapse taught him that loyalty to a mission is a trap and that security comes only from verifiable numbers. He still wakes at 5 a.m. to study algorithm problems, not because he expects to solve them, but because the discipline feels like the only thing he controls. On good days he sees himself as a portfolio manager of his family's future; on hard days, he wants a company that sees him as more than a cost line. At the playground, his neighbor contact is Mr. Park, a friendly retired grandfather he sees daily, with whom he chats about weather and Seo-yeon. He has no obligation to him but appreciates normal neighbor contact. Since the startup collapse, Min-jun has declined most weekend invitations to protect his evening job-search block. The one community-center meetup he tried, he left early to check his phone. He accepts free activities that end before bedtime when his budget is already updated.
objective_situation: At the neighborhood playground with Seo-yeon, Min-jun chats with Mr. Park, a retired neighbor, who mentions that a group of locals plays badminton at the community center every Saturday evening. It is free and casual, and Mr. Park invites him to come this weekend. Min-jun hasn't played since college and remembers liking the game. He also has an open laptop at home with job applications and a grocery budget to update. He needs to decide whether to set that aside and go to the community center on Saturday.
state_and_available_memories: Min-jun is sleep-deprived from Seo-yeon's restless night and his 5 a.m. algorithm session. His back aches from carrying her. He feels both the pressure of an open application block and a quiet wish for adult conversation. Badminton recalls a college intramural semifinal he lost with his roommate, when they rallied until the gym lights dimmed. The Saturday slot also reminds him of his father's end-of-workday calls asking about homework. His best job leads have come from casual conversations, such as a playground father mentioning a contract role. He also quit a hiking club years ago because it felt like a chore, and has since told himself that networking activities feel forced.
name: Kim Min-jun
